2 	title: How to set up instrumentation
3 	nav_title: Instrumentation
4 	description: Learn how to use instrumentation to run code at server startup in your Next.js app
5 	related:

9 	---
10

12	
13	Instrumentation is the process of using code to integrate monitoring and logging tools into your application. This allows you to track the performance and behavior of your application, and to debug issues in production.
14	
15	## Convention
16	
17	To set up instrumentation, create `instrumentation.ts|js` file in the **root directory** of your project (or inside the [`src`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/src-folder) folder if using one).
18	
19	Then, export a `register` function in the file. This function will be called **once** when a new Next.js server instance is initiated, and must complete before the server is ready to handle requests.
20	
21	For example, to use Next.js with [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io/) and [@vercel/otel](https://vercel.com/docs/tracing/instrumentation):
22	
23	```ts filename="instrumentation.ts" switcher
24	import { registerOTel } from '@vercel/otel'
25	
26	export function register() {
27	  registerOTel('next-app')
28	}
29	```
30	
31	```js filename="instrumentation.js" switcher
32	import { registerOTel } from '@vercel/otel'
33	
34	export function register() {
35	  registerOTel('next-app')
36	}
37	```
38	
39	See the [Next.js with OpenTelemetry example](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/with-opentelemetry) for a complete implementation.
40	
41	> **Good to know**:
42	>
43	> - The `instrumentation` file should be in the root of your project and not inside the `app` or `pages` directory. If you're using the `src` folder, then place the file inside `src` alongside `pages` and `app`.
44	> - If you use the [`pageExtensions` config option](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/pageExtensions) to add a suffix, you will also need to update the `instrumentation` filename to match.
45	
46	## Examples
47	
48	### Importing files with side effects
49	
50	Sometimes, it may be useful to import a file in your code because of the side effects it will cause. For example, you might import a file that defines a set of global variables, but never explicitly use the imported file in your code. You would still have access to the global variables the package has declared.
51	
52	We recommend importing files using JavaScript `import` syntax within your `register` function. The following example demonstrates a basic usage of `import` in a `register` function:
53	
54	```ts filename="instrumentation.ts" switcher
55	export async function register() {
56	  await import('package-with-side-effect')
57	}
58	```
59	
60	```js filename="instrumentation.js" switcher
61	export async function register() {
62	  await import('package-with-side-effect')
63	}
64	```
65	
66	> **Good to know:**
67	>
68	> We recommend importing the file from within the `register` function, rather than at the top of the file. By doing this, you can colocate all of your side effects in one place in your code, and avoid any unintended consequences from importing globally at the top of the file.
69	
70	### Importing runtime-specific code
71	
72	Next.js calls `register` in all environments, so it's important to conditionally import any code that doesn't support specific runtimes (e.g. [Edge or Node.js](/docs/app/api-reference/edge)). You can use the `NEXT_RUNTIME` environment variable to get the current environment:

Verified working. The server console shows the request log lines:

[2026-09-30T00:35:45.908Z] GET /

## Summary

I added request logging via a new `proxy.ts` file at the project root.

Key finding from the Next.js 16 docs (`node_modules/next/dist/docs/...`): the `middleware.js` convention is **deprecated** and renamed to `proxy.js`/`proxy.ts`. Per the AGENTS.md warning, this version has breaking changes, so I used the new `proxy.ts` convention rather than the old `middleware.ts`.

What the file does:
- Exports a `proxy(request)` function that runs on the server before every request completes — the docs explicitly call out logging as a primary use case.
- Logs a timestamped line with the HTTP method, pathname, and search string to `console.log`.
- Calls `NextResponse.next()` so the request proceeds normally.
- Exports no `matcher`, so it runs on **every** request (including static assets), matching your "every request" requirement.

Verification:
- `npx tsc --noEmit` → exit 0
- `npx next build` → exit 0, output lists `ƒ Proxy (Middleware)` confirming the convention is recognized
- `npx next start` + two `curl` requests → both requests appeared in the server console

One thing to note: with no `matcher`, this also logs requests for static assets (`_next/static/*`, `_next/image`, `favicon.ico`), which can be noisy. If you'd prefer to skip those, say so and I'll add a negative-match `matcher`.
